claim: Place cells of the rodent hippocampus fire action potentials when the animal traverses a particular spatial location in any environment.
source: Place cells of the rodent hippocampus fire action potentials when the animal traverses a particular spatial location in any environment.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations in the introduction (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and O'Keefe, 1976; Harvey et al., 2009).

claim: For any given trajectory one observes a repeatable sequence of place cell activations.
source: Therefore for any given trajectory one observes a repeatable sequence of place cell activations.
evidence: This follows logically from the fact that place cells fire at specific locations, and is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: When the animal is quiescent or sleeping, one can observe similar sequences of activation known as replay.
source: When the animal is quiescent or sleeping, one can observe similar sequences of activation known as replay, which underlie the process of memory consolidation.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011).

claim: Replay underlies the process of memory consolidation.
source: When the animal is quiescent or sleeping, one can observe similar sequences of activation known as replay, which underlie the process of memory consolidation.
evidence: This is a widely accepted hypothesis in the field, supported by the literature on replay.

claim: A temporally asymmetric plasticity rule during spatial exploration gives rise to spontaneous replay in a model network.
source: Here we show how a temporally asymmetric plasticity rule during spatial exploration gives rise to spontaneous replay in a model network by shaping the recurrent connectivity to reflect the topology of the learned environment.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the computational model presented in the manuscript, demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The temporally asymmetric plasticity rule shapes the recurrent connectivity to reflect the topology of the learned environment.
source: Here we show how a temporally asymmetric plasticity rule during spatial exploration gives rise to spontaneous replay in a model network by shaping the recurrent connectivity to reflect the topology of the learned environment.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model through the evolution of connectivity patterns shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The rate of encoding is strongly modulated by ongoing rhythms.
source: Crucially, the rate of this encoding is strongly modulated by ongoing rhythms.
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated in Figure 4 showing the dependence of learning rate on modulation frequency.

claim: Oscillations in the theta range optimize learning by generating repeated pre-post pairings on a time-scale commensurate with the window for plasticity.
source: Oscillations in the theta range optimize learning by generating repeated pre-post pairings on a time-scale commensurate with the window for plasticity, while lower and higher frequencies generate learning rates which are lower by orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is demonstrated through both simulations (Figure 4) and theoretical analysis (Figure 5).

claim: Lower and higher frequencies than theta generate learning rates which are lower by orders of magnitude.
source: Oscillations in the theta range optimize learning by generating repeated pre-post pairings on a time-scale commensurate with the window for plasticity, while lower and higher frequencies generate learning rates which are lower by orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is shown quantitatively in Figure 4ai where the even mode amplitude varies by orders of magnitude across frequencies.

claim: Place cells in the hippocampus fire selectively at particular locations known as 'place-fields'.
source: As an animal explores in any given environment, place cells in the hippocampus fire selectively at particular locations (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and O'Keefe, 1976; Harvey et al., 2009), known as the 'place-fields' of the cells.
evidence: This is supported by the cited foundational studies in place cell research.

claim: Place fields of an ensemble of place cells remap to completely new positions with respect to one another if the animal enters a distinct environment.
source: Furthermore, the place fields of an ensemble of place cells remap to completely new positions with respect to one another if the animal enters a distinct environment (Muller and Kubie, 1987; Kubie and Muller, 1991; Bostock et al., 1991).
evidence: This phenomenon of global remapping is well-documented in the cited literature.

claim: Sequential place cell activation during exploration acts as a unique fingerprint for each environment.
source: Sequential place cell activation during exploration therefore acts as a unique fingerprint for each environment, providing information needed for navigation and spatial learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of place cells and remapping described in the literature.

claim: Spontaneous replay of sequential activation occurs within sharp-wave/ripples during quiet wakefulness.
source: The spontaneous replay of such sequential activation, which occurs within sharp-wave/ripples (SWRs) during quiet wakefulness (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011) and sleep (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Lee and Wilson, 2002) suggests that the animal has formed an internal representation of the corresponding environment, presumably during exploration (Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies on replay.

claim: Spontaneous replay of sequential activation occurs during sleep.
source: The spontaneous replay of such sequential activation, which occurs within sharp-wave/ripples (SWRs) during quiet wakefulness (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011) and sleep (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Lee and Wilson, 2002) suggests that the animal has formed an internal representation of the corresponding environment, presumably during exploration (Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies on replay during sleep.

claim: Replay suggests that the animal has formed an internal representation of the corresponding environment during exploration.
source: The spontaneous replay of such sequential activation, which occurs within sharp-wave/ripples (SWRs) during quiet wakefulness (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011) and sleep (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Lee and Wilson, 2002) suggests that the animal has formed an internal representation of the corresponding environment, presumably during exploration (Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by the cited literature on replay and memory.

claim: Synaptic plasticity is the clear candidate mechanism for the formation of internal representations.
source: Synaptic plasticity is the clear candidate mechanism for this formation.
evidence: This is based on established neuroscience knowledge about learning and memory mechanisms.

claim: It remains unclear how changes in synaptic connectivity are coordinated at the network level to generate well-ordered sequences spontaneously.
source: Nonetheless it remains unclear how changes in the synaptic connectivity are coordinated at the network level in order to generate well-ordered sequences spontaneously.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current understanding that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: The theta rhythm (4–12 Hz) is a prominent physiological signature of exploratory behavior in the hippocampus.
source: An additional prominent physiological signature of exploratory behavior in the hippocampus is the theta rhythm (4–12 Hz).
evidence: This is well-established knowledge in hippocampal physiology.

claim: Decreases in theta power due to lesions of the medial septum strongly reduce performance in spatial-memory based tasks.
source: Decreases in theta power due to lesions of the medial septum strongly reduce performance in spatial-memory based tasks (Winson, 1978; Mitchell et al., 1982; Dwyer et al., 2007) and other hippocampal dependent tasks (Berry and Thompson, 1979; Allen et al., 2002) although they do not eliminate place fields on linear tracks (Brandon et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies on medial septum lesions.

claim: Medial septum lesions do not eliminate place fields on linear tracks.
source: Decreases in theta power due to lesions of the medial septum strongly reduce performance in spatial-memory based tasks (Winson, 1978; Mitchell et al., 1982; Dwyer et al., 2007) and other hippocampal dependent tasks (Berry and Thompson, 1979; Allen et al., 2002) although they do not eliminate place fields on linear tracks (Brandon et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Lesioned animals can still reach fixed performance criteria given enough time.
source: Despite this, lesioned animals can still reach fixed performance criteria given enough time (Winson, 1978; Berry and Thompson, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Theta is important for learning and may act as a dial for the learning rate.
source: This shows not only that theta is important for learning, but also suggests a potential mechanism. Namely, it may act as a dial for the learning rate, presumably by modulating the network-wide coordination of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about theta and learning performance.

claim: The model network consists of recurrently coupled, excitatory stochastic firing rate neurons.
source: The model consisted of recurrently coupled, excitatory stochastic firing rate neurons, each of which received a place-specific external input on any given track, and inhibition was modeled as a global inhibitory feedback, see Materials and methods for model details.
evidence: This describes the computational model architecture used in the study.

claim: Each neuron in the model received a place-specific external input on any given track.
source: The model consisted of recurrently coupled, excitatory stochastic firing rate neurons, each of which received a place-specific external input on any given track, and inhibition was modeled as a global inhibitory feedback, see Materials and methods for model details.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model design.

claim: Inhibition was modeled as a global inhibitory feedback.
source: The model consisted of recurrently coupled, excitatory stochastic firing rate neurons, each of which received a place-specific external input on any given track, and inhibition was modeled as a global inhibitory feedback, see Materials and methods for model details.
evidence: This describes how inhibition was implemented in the model.

claim: The position of the peak input and place field of each neuron was randomized to model global remapping from one track to another.
source: To model the global remapping of place fields from one track to another, we randomized the position of the peak input, and as a consequence the place field, of each neuron.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach for global remapping.

claim: The ordering of cells according to their place field location on one track was random and uncorrelated with their ordering on any other track.
source: In this way, the ordering of cells according to their place field location on one track was random and uncorrelated with their ordering on any other track, see Figure 1b.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b and describes a key property of the model.

claim: A 'balanced' plasticity rule was considered, for which the degree of potentiation and depression were the same on average given constant firing rates.
source: We also considered a 'balanced' plasticity rule, for which the degree of potentiation and depression were the same, on average, given constant firing rates.
evidence: This describes a property of the plasticity rule used in the model.

claim: A balanced plasticity rule is a means of avoiding fully potentiating or fully depressing all synapses on long time-scales.
source: Such a rule is a means of avoiding fully potentiating or fully depressing all synapses on long time-scales, that is it allows for the generation and maintenance of structured synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This explains the rationale for using a balanced plasticity rule.

claim: The network was exposed to a series of distinct tracks until the matrix of recurrent synaptic weights no longer depended on its initial state.
source: In order to study 'typical' place-cell dynamics during exploration we first exposed the network to a series of distinct tracks until the matrix of recurrent synaptic weights no longer depended on its initial state.
evidence: This describes the training procedure for the model.

claim: After exploring 10 tracks, the network was exposed to another novel track and the dynamics were studied in detail.
source: After exploring 10 tracks, we exposed the network to another novel track and studied the dynamics in detail; because the exploration process had already become largely stereotyped (despite some variability), the dynamics on the novel track reflected what would be seen qualitatively during the exploration of any other novel track in the future, that is it was dependent only on the learning process itself and not the initial state of the synaptic weight matrix.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for studying learning on a novel track.

claim: The external input was maximal for cells with place fields at the animal's current position and minimal for cells with place fields at the opposite side of the track.
source: Specifically, the external input was maximal for cells with place fields at the animal's current position and minimal for cells with place fields at the opposite side of the track, with the input decaying smoothly for intermediate locations like a cosine curve, see Materials and methods for details.
evidence: This describes how place field input was modeled.

claim: The velocity of the virtual animal was modeled as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a time constant of 10 s.
source: We modeled the motion of the animal by taking the velocity to be an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a time constant of 10 s; this lead to realistic trajectories with changes of direction, see Figure 2—figure supplement 3.
evidence: This describes the motion model used in simulations, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Every three minutes of simulation time the virtual animal was stopped at its current location for three seconds and the place field input was removed.
source: Every three minutes of simulation time we stopped the animal at its current location for three seconds and removed the place field input.
evidence: This describes the protocol for simulating awake quiescence periods.

claim: Removing place field input led to spontaneous bursting via a synaptic depression-dependent mechanism.
source: This led to spontaneous bursting via a synaptic depression-dependent mechanism (Romani and Tsodyks, 2015), reminiscent of sharp-waves seen during awake quiescence and sleep, see Figure 2.
evidence: This describes the mechanism for generating spontaneous bursts, shown in Figure 2 and supported by citation.

claim: Synaptic plasticity was allowed to occur during both theta activity and sharp-waves.
source: Synaptic plasticity was allowed to occur during both theta activity and sharp-waves, that is it was never 'turned-off'.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model implementation.

claim: During early exploration, the connectivity is not correlated with the place-field ordering.
source: During early exploration, the connectivity is not correlated with the place-field ordering, while during late exploration cells with neighboring place-fields are more strongly connected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a through snapshots of connectivity at different times.

claim: During late exploration cells with neighboring place-fields are more strongly connected.
source: During early exploration, the connectivity is not correlated with the place-field ordering, while during late exploration cells with neighboring place-fields are more strongly connected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a through snapshots of connectivity at different times.

claim: The sequential correlation (SC) during theta-activity was already non-zero at the outset of the simulation by virtue of the external place-field input.
source: The SC during theta-activity (exploration) was already non-zero at the outset of the simulation by virtue of the external place-field input which generates sequential activity, black squares Figure 2b.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b and explained by the presence of place field input.

claim: The SC was initially near zero during spontaneous bursts.
source: On the other hand, the SC was initially near zero during spontaneous bursts, red circles Figure 2b.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The SC abruptly increased during burst activity at a critical time and remained elevated for the duration of the simulation.
source: Interestingly the SC abruptly increased during burst activity at a critical time and remained elevated for the duration of the simulation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b and represents a key finding of the model.

claim: The transition in SC occurred even in simulations with strong heterogeneity in place field tuning.
source: This transition occurred even in simulations where we included strong heterogeneity in place field tuning, see Figure 2—figure supplement 4.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The SC for theta-activity showed a steady increase leading up to the transition.
source: Note that the SC for theta-activity also showed a steady increase leading up to this transition, as did the SC when the total activity was taken into account, without discerning between epochs of movement or awake quiescence, see Figure 2b inset.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b inset.

claim: The steady increase in SC is due to the emergence of theta sequences.
source: This steady increase is due to the emergence of so-called theta sequences (Foster and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: This is explained by reference to theta sequences and supported by citation.

claim: Theta sequences are bursts of place-cell activity which sweep ahead of the animal's position on every theta cycle during awake exploration.
source: These are bursts of place-cell activity which sweep ahead of the animal's position on every theta cycle during awake exploration, see Figure 2—figure supplement 5.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and supported by citation.

claim: The emergence of theta sequences coincides with a precession of the phase of the underlying firing rate with the ongoing theta rhythm.
source: The emergence of theta sequences here also coincides with a precession of the phase of the underlying firing rate with the ongoing theta rhythm, see Figure 2—figure supplement 5f and discussion for more detail.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5f.

claim: The abrupt increase in SC coincides with a transition in the spatio-temporal structure of the bursts.
source: Space-time plots of place-cell activity show that the abrupt increase in SC coincides with a transition in the spatio-temporal structure of the bursts: it is initially uncorrelated with the ordering of cells on the novel track, Figure 2c (i), and after the transition there is a clear sequential activation reminiscent of so-called 'replay' activity, Figure 2c (ii).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c through space-time plots before and after the transition.

claim: Before the transition, bursts are highly structured but correlated with a previously explored track and not the novel one.
source: In fact, before the transition the bursts are highly structured, but this structure is correlated with a previously explored track and not the novel one.
evidence: This is an observation from the model simulations.

claim: If the learning process was carried on for much longer times all relevant network properties saturated.
source: In fact, before the transition the bursts are highly structured, but this structure is correlated with a previously explored track and not the novel one. If the learning process was carried on for much longer times all relevant network properties, such as connectivity and mean firing rates, saturated, see Figure 2—figure supplement 8.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The transition in burst activity always occurred when the coefficient of the first even mode reached a critical value.
source: We tracked these modes in time and discovered that the transition in burst activity always occurred when the coefficient of the first even mode reached a critical value.
evidence: This is a key finding from tracking Fourier modes of connectivity over time.

claim: There is an instability of the spontaneous activity to bursts when the even mode of the connectivity times the gain in the neuronal transfer function is greater than a critical value.
source: In fact, a theoretical analysis of our model shows that there is an instability of the spontaneous activity to bursts when the even mode of the connectivity times the gain in the neuronal transfer function is greater than a critical value, see Materials and methods.
evidence: This is derived from theoretical analysis presented in Materials and methods.

claim: The gain in the transfer function was nearly always the same during bursts because it depended on the mean input to the network during quiescence, which was constant.
source: In our simulations the gain in the transfer function was nearly always the same during bursts because it depended on the mean input to the network during quiescence, which was constant.
evidence: This is an observation from the model simulations.

claim: It was principally the even mode of the recurrent connectivity which determined the time of the transition.
source: Therefore it was principally the even mode of the recurrent connectivity which determined the time of the transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the constancy of the gain and the dependence on the even mode.

claim: The transition to replay occurred when the coefficient of the even mode reached a critical value as seen in Figure 3c.
source: For this reason, the transition to replay occurred when the coefficient of the even mode reached a critical value as seen in Figure 3c.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c.

claim: There was no dependence of the transition on the odd mode.
source: Note that there was no such dependence on the odd mode (dotted lines in Figure 3c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The growth of the even mode depended strongly on the frequency, peaking at an intermediate range and decreasing by orders of magnitude at low and high frequencies.
source: We then asked how the growth of the even mode depended on the details of the plasticity rule and the frequency of periodic modulation of the place cell activity. We found that the growth of the even mode depended strongly on the frequency, peaking at an intermediate range and decreasing by orders of magnitude at low and high frequencies, Figure 4ai.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4ai.

claim: The frequency dependence of even mode growth occurred independent of the details of the animal's motion.
source: This occurred independent of the details of the animal's motion, for example compare Figure 4ai and Figure 2—figure supplement 2e for irregular versus purely clockwise motion respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing results from different motion patterns.

claim: The odd mode closely tracks the cumulative bias in the animal's motion and is independent of the forcing frequency to leading order.
source: On the other hand the odd mode, which represents a directional bias in the recurrent connectivity, closely tracks the cumulative bias in the animal's motion, see Figure 2—figure supplement 3, and is independent of the forcing frequency to leading order, see Materials and methods for details.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and derived theoretically.

claim: For simulations of up to 1 hr, transitions in burst activity were observed only when the frequency was in the range of 2–10 Hz.
source: The strong dependence of the growth of the even mode on frequency, meant that, for simulations of up to 1 hr, transitions in the burst activity were observed only when the frequency was in the range of 2–10 Hz, Figure 4aii.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4aii.

claim: The even mode only grew when the plasticity rule had dominant potentiation at short latencies.
source: Furthermore, the even mode only grew, and transitions only occurred, when the plasticity rule had dominant potentiation at short latencies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing different plasticity rules in Figure 4.

claim: For a perfectly anti-symmetric plasticity rule, the even mode did not change.
source: For a perfectly anti-symmetric plasticity rule, and for a rule with dominant inhibition at short latencies, the even mode did not change and even decreased, respectively, Figure 4b and c.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4b.

claim: For a rule with dominant depression at short latencies, bursts were suppressed entirely.
source: In the latter case bursts were suppressed entirely (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from simulations.

claim: The learning rate during exploration depends almost entirely on the product of the autocorrelation of place-cell activity and the window for plasticity.
source: Our major finding is that the learning rate during the exploration of a novel environment depends almost entirely on the product of the autocorrelation of place-cell activity and the window for plasticity.
evidence: This is derived from theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The integral of the product of autocorrelation and plasticity window determines the growth rate of a global, network-wide pattern of synaptic connectivity.
source: The integral of this product determines the growth rate of a global, network-wide pattern of synaptic connectivity, which results in strong local recurrence and long-range competition.
evidence: This is derived from theoretical analysis, specifically Equation 5.

claim: The growth rate of the connectivity mode is maximum when place-cell activity is periodically modulated on a time-scale commensurate with the plasticity rule.
source: The growth rate of this mode is maximum when place-cell activity is periodically modulated on a time-scale commensurate with the plasticity rule, which for realistic time constants yields frequencies in the theta range.
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Lower and higher frequencies than theta lead to learning rates which are orders of magnitude slower.
source: Furthermore, lower and higher frequencies than theta lead to learning rates which are orders of magnitude slower.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: The role of theta is to accelerate learning.
source: This suggests that the role of theta is to accelerate learning.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed based on the model findings.

claim: The overall rate of plasticity is not affected by the presence of oscillations.
source: Note that the overall rate of plasticity is not affected by the presence of oscillations. The number of spike pairs, and hence the number of potentiations and depressions, depends only on the firing rates.
evidence: This is explained as a key insight about the mechanism.

claim: Theta oscillations generate repeated pre-post pairings in both directions, which coupled with a plasticity rule with dominant potentiation at short latencies bias plasticity toward potentiating events for neurons with neighboring place fields.
source: Rather, theta oscillations generate repeated pre-post pairings in both directions, which coupled with a plasticity rule with dominant potentiation at short latencies bias plasticity toward potentiating events for neurons with neighboring place fields.
evidence: This explains the mechanism by which theta affects learning.

claim: One signature of the learning mechanism is a continuous increase in the pairwise cross-correlation in the activity of neighboring place-cells leading up to a critical time.
source: One signature of this mechanism is a continuous increase in the pairwise cross-correlation in the activity of neighboring place-cells leading up to a critical time.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Evidence consistent with increased pairwise cross-correlation was found by analyzing the activity of simultaneously recorded hippocampal place cells in a rat during exploration of a novel track.
source: We have found evidence consistent with this by analyzing the activity of simultaneously recorded hippocampal place cells in a rat during the exploration of a novel track.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data analysis presented in Figure 7.

claim: Pairwise reactivations of CA1 place-cells with overlapping place fields during awake SWRs improve during exploration.
source: Pairwise reactivations of CA1 place-cells with overlapping place fields during awake SWRs improve during exploration; they are stronger during late exploration than early exploration (O'Neill et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental study.

claim: Reactivations of entire neuronal ensembles improve during exploration on linear tracks.
source: This holds true not only for pairwise correlations, but also reactivations of entire neuronal ensembles, at least on linear tracks (Jackson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental study.

claim: Significant replay events during awake SWRs in rats running along a three-arm maze emerge abruptly only after a certain number of runs.
source: More recent work has shown that significant replay events during awake SWRs in rats running along a three-arm maze emerge abruptly only after a certain number of runs (Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental study.

claim: Cells with well-defined place fields were identified by extracting the coefficients and phase of the first two spatial Fourier modes of their time-averaged activity.
source: We first identified cells with well-defined place fields by extracting the coefficients and phase of the first two spatial Fourier modes of their time-averaged activity as a function of the normalized distance along the track (in radians), see Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3.
evidence: This describes the method used for data analysis.

claim: Only cells for which the Tuning Index (TI) exceeded the threshold of one were kept, indicating strong spatially selective activity.
source: We kept only those cells for which the ratio of the coefficients, the Tuning Index (TI), exceeded the threshold of one, indicating strong spatially selective activity, see methods for details.
evidence: This describes the selection criterion for well-tuned place cells.

claim: The SC of activity over the total duration of the experiment using the proper ordering was significantly higher than 5000 randomly reshuffled orderings.
source: The SC of activity over the total duration of the experiment using this ordering was significantly higher than 5000 randomly reshuffled orderings which on average gave SC = 0, see Figure 7a and b.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a and b.

claim: The time course of SC given the proper ordering does not show any dynamics when the medial septum is reversibly inactivated with muscimol.
source: The time course of SC given the proper ordering (solid symbols) does not show any dynamics when the medial septum is reversibly inactivated with muscimol.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Place fields are intact even though theta is disrupted during muscimol inactivation.
source: Note, however, the clear separation with the shuffled data (open symbols), indicating that place fields are intact even though theta is disrupted.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7c.

claim: After recovery from muscimol, the SC exhibits a significant increase over the first 10 minutes of exploration and then plateaus.
source: After a rest period the animal is placed back onto the same track; the SC now exhibits a significant increase given the proper ordering (solid symbols) over the first 10 min of exploration and then plateaus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7d.

claim: There is a large reduction of theta power in the muscimol condition compared to post-muscimol.
source: Note that the bottom plots in (c) and (d) show the power spectrum of hippocampal LFP (CA1), indicating a large reduction of theta power in the muscimol condition.
evidence: This is shown in the bottom plots of Figure 7c and d.

claim: When the animal explores a novel track, there is a significant increase in the SC only during the first session.
source: When the animal is allowed to explore a novel track and then placed back on the track for a second and third session, there is a significant increase in the SC only during the first session.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The increase in correlation only occurred when the environment was novel.
source: Furthermore, no such increase was found on subsequent sessions on the same track, indicating that the change in correlation only occurred when the environment was novel.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison across sessions in Figure 7e.

claim: There is no global change in neuronal correlations during exploration that could occur due to slow changes in theta modulation or neuronal excitability.
source: This indicates that there are no global changes in neuronal correlations during exploration, which could occur, for example, due to slow changes in theta modulation or neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between proper and shuffled orderings.

claim: There is a sustained increase in pairwise correlations only between neurons which encode nearby places, and only when strong theta modulation is present.
source: Rather, there is a sustained increase in pairwise correlations only between those neurons which encode nearby places, and only when strong theta modulation is present.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Sparse coding allows for the replay of activity from multiple explored tracks during bursts.
source: The spatio-temporal structure of sharp-wave-like bursts in our model reflected the sequential ordering of place fields on the most recently explored track; correlation with earlier tracks was erased or greatly reduced. In reality, only a fraction of place cells have well-defined place fields in any given environment, that is coding is sparse (Bostock et al., 1991; Fyhn et al., 2007). We incorporated this sparse-coding strategy to our model by providing place-field input to only one half of the total neurons in the network; the other half received constant input.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model with sparse coding shown in Figure 6.

claim: The resulting matrix of synaptic connections with sparse coding was correlated with the ordering of place-cells in several past explored environments.
source: We then allowed the network to evolve by having the virtual animal explore thirty distinct tracks, each for 1 hr of simulation time, as before. The resulting matrix of synaptic connections was correlated with the ordering of place-cells in several past explored environments, Figure 6a.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The amplitude of the even mode decayed roughly exponentially as a function of the recency of the explored track.
source: The amplitude of the even mode, which is responsible for generating spontaneous replay, decayed roughly exponentially as a function of the recency of the explored track, Figure 6a inset.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a inset.

claim: When the network was driven with a global, non-selective input, the replay was strongly correlated with the past two explored environments.
source: Indeed, when the network was driven with a global, non-selective input, the replay was strongly correlated with the past two explored environments, Figure 6b, whereas the correlation with earlier environments was negligible.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b.

claim: When the constant external drive was selective to the subset of place-cells on any given track, replay activity was robustly correlated with activity on that track only.
source: On the other hand, when the constant external drive was selective to the subset of place-cells on any given track, replay activity was robustly correlated with activity on that track only, Figure 6c.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Selective input may originate in cortical circuits which store environment-specific sensory information as stable patterns of activity.
source: Such selective input may originate in cortical circuits which store environment-specific sensory information as stable patterns of activity; these patterns correspond to attracting fixed points in network models of long-term memory storage and memory recall (Hopfield, 1982; Tsodyks and Feigel'man, 1988; Recanatesi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to memory models.

claim: Spontaneous switching between cortical representations during slow-wave activity would engage distinct hippocampal replay patterns, which could strengthen and consolidate the corresponding cortical memory trace.
source: Spontaneous switching between cortical representations during slow-wave activity would therefore engage distinct hippocampal replay patterns, which in turn could strengthen and consolidate the corresponding cortical memory trace.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the functional role of the mechanism.

claim: The number of different environments which could be simultaneously encoded in replay depended on model details, particularly the coding level.
source: The number of different environments which could be simultaneously encoded in replay depended on model details, particularly the coding level, that is the fraction of active place cells in any given environment (not shown) (Battaglia and Treves, 1998).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from simulations and supported by citation.
